findings.claim: Majority of duodenal NETs are non-functional -> incidentally discovered on endoscopy
findings.verbatim_support: With a progressive increase in endoscopy procedures, pathologists are bound to see an increased number of duodenal NETs in their routine clinical practice. The majority of these are non-functional; hence, many are incidentally discovered on endoscopy. The existing data describe them endoscopically as small, sessile erythematous or pale lesions or submucosal hemispherical or flatly elevated lesions that can be seen in the duodenal cap, bulb, first or second part of the duodenum. However, in routine clinical practice, we have seen them as lumped together and often described as a mucosal or submucosal nodule. In addition to NETs, a 'nodular' endoscopic appearance can have varied histological differentials, including benign aetiologies such as Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis and lymphoid hyperplasia, among others. Once diagnosed there is very limited evidence for a wait-and-watch policy, and it is generally recommended that the tumour be completely excised using endoscopic resection or even local resection, if endoscopic therapy is high risk or unlikely to be curative. Treatment is based on tumour size, location, histological grade, stage and tumour type. Given that metastases to lymph nodes and liver from duodenal NET are known to occur and even patients with tumour size ≤ 1 cm have a 40% chance of nodal metastases, an early and accurate diagnosis is essential. The pathological assessment and grading of duodenal NETs is akin to NETs at other GI sites.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk introduces the clinical and pathological landscape of duodenal neuroendocrine tumours (NETs). The majority of duodenal NETs are non-functional and are incidentally discovered on endoscopy [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Endoscopically, they manifest as small, sessile, erythematous or pale lesions, or as submucosal hemispherical/flatly elevated lesions in the duodenal cap, bulb, or first/second part of the duodenum [S3|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. The differential diagnosis for a nodular duodenal appearance includes benign entities such as Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis, and lymphoid hyperplasia [S5|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Evidence for a wait-and-watch policy is very limited; complete excision via endoscopic or local resection is generally recommended [S6|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Treatment decisions are driven by tumour size, location, histological grade, stage, and tumour type [S7|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Critically, duodenal NETs metastasise to lymph nodes and liver, and even tumours ≤1 cm carry a 40% risk of nodal metastases [S8|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Pathological grading is performed analogously to NETs at other GI sites [S9|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799].

findings.claim: Duodenal NETs -> present as mucosal or submucosal nodules; peptic duodenitis can confound by producing nodular appearance
findings.verbatim_support: To summarise, pathologists should always consider a possibility of NET when encountered with a duodenal mucosal or submucosal nodule, despite the presence of other confounding aetiologies, such as peptic duodenitis, that can account in part for the 'nodular' appearance. Pathologists need to be cognisant that NETs in duodenum can show crush artefact with crushed tumour cells mimicking crushed lymphoid cells, a diagnostic pitfall. Another pitfall is that these tumour cells can also mimic Brunner glands; however, the presence of Brunner-like glands in the superficial mucosa or showing an infiltrative appearing pattern should alert pathologists to consider the possibility of NET.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk provides diagnostic guidance on duodenal neuroendocrine tumours (NETs). First, any duodenal mucosal or submucosal nodule warrants consideration of NET even when confounders such as peptic duodenitis are present [S1|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4800]. Second, a key diagnostic pitfall is that duodenal NETs can exhibit crush artefact, causing tumour cells to morphologically resemble crushed lymphoid cells [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4800]. Third, duodenal NET tumour cells may mimic Brunner glands; however, Brunner-like glands located in the superficial mucosa or displaying an infiltrative growth pattern should raise suspicion for NET [S3|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4800].
